draft.title: Jewish practice
card: The Sabbath runs from Friday evening to Saturday evening each week. It is a day of rest, when observant Jews stop everyday work and spend time on prayer, family and community.
Keeping kosher means following Jewish food laws. These set out which foods may be eaten and how food is prepared. Pork and shellfish are not kosher, and meat and dairy are kept apart.
Jews mark festivals through the year. Passover (Pesach) remembers the Israelites' escape from slavery in Egypt. Families hold a meal called a seder and eat matzah, a flat unleavened bread.
These practices are ways of living out the commandments in daily and yearly life. They also link Jews to their history and to each other.
draft.remember: Shabbat, kosher food and festivals such as Passover turn Jewish belief into regular practice.

a.q: Which practice is a weekly day of rest from Friday evening to Saturday evening?
a.why: Shabbat is the weekly day of rest that begins on Friday evening. Passover is a festival held once a year, so it is the tempting wrong answer. Kashrut is about food laws, not a day of rest.
a.clue: Think of the one that happens every week.

b.q: Dani's family in Melbourne gathers for a meal, eats matzah and retells the escape from slavery in Egypt. Which practice are they observing?
b.why: Matzah and the retelling of the escape from Egypt belong to Passover, and the meal is called a seder. Shabbat is tempting because it also involves family meals. But Shabbat is a weekly day of rest and does not centre on the escape from Egypt.
b.clue: Which practice remembers the escape from slavery?
